issues.legal_issue: A government offer of land at a concessional rate to encourage industrial development does not establish the land’s market value for compensation.
material_facts: The government offered land in an adjacent industrial area to industrialists at a concessional rate to induce them to establish factories.
The acquired land was near the industrial area and had potential for non-agricultural use.
issues.conclusion: The concessional rate was not evidence of the prevailing market value because the offer was intended as an inducement and did not reflect a transaction between willing buyers and willing sellers.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, compensation is based on market value, meaning the price a willing purchaser would pay a willing seller having regard to the land’s advantages, nearby development and potentiality. A concession offered to induce industrial development does not represent that market value.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: An owner appealed the compensation determined for land acquired by the government.
predicates.offer_was_inducement_rate: The government offered land at a reduced rate to encourage industrialists to establish businesses in the area.
predicates.transaction_was_not_market_sale: The reduced-rate offer was not a sale reflecting the price agreed between a willing seller and a willing purchaser.

issues.definition: When an owner appeals compensation for acquired land and the government’s reduced-rate offer was an inducement rather than a market sale, the offer is not evidence of market value.

issues.legal_issue: An earlier purchase price does not cap compensation when the land lacked potential at the time of purchase and later development increased its value.
material_facts: The land had been purchased when the nearby industrial area had not yet developed and the land lacked the later potential for industrial or building use.
By the time of acquisition, the land was near a developed industrial area and was suitable for non-agricultural use.
issues.conclusion: The earlier purchase price did not justify limiting compensation because the land’s potential and value had increased after the purchase.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires compensation based on market value, assessed with regard to the land’s advantages, development in the vicinity and potentiality. An earlier purchase price from a period when the land lacked that potential does not control the later market value.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: An owner appealed the compensation determined for land acquired by the government.
predicates.earlier_purchase_preceded_development: The land was purchased before development in its vicinity had occurred.
predicates.land_later_gained_potentiality: By the time of acquisition, the land had gained development-related potential for more valuable uses.

issues.definition: When acquired land was purchased before nearby development and later gained potential for more valuable uses, its earlier purchase price does not cap compensation.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation should not be reduced below that awarded for materially similar adjacent land when no material difference in the land is shown.
material_facts: The acquired land was adjacent to other land for which compensation had been fixed at a higher rate in decisions concerning the same acquisition area.
The respondents did not identify a material difference in situation, topography or layout between the acquired land and the adjacent land.
The evidence showed that the acquired land was near an industrial area, was suitable for non-agricultural use and had future potential as a factory or building site.
issues.conclusion: The landowners were entitled to compensation at the same rate as for the materially similar adjacent land, and the reduced award was set aside. The Court relied on the High Court’s decisions concerning adjacent plots, including Collector, Cuttack v. Karunakar Mahanty, First Appeals Nos. 173 and 174 of 1971, decided October 21, 1975.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires compensation based on market value, including the land’s advantages, nearby development and potentiality. The Court considered the High Court’s awards for adjacent plots, including Collector, Cuttack v. Karunakar Mahanty, and found no material difference that justified a lower valuation.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: An owner appealed the compensation determined for land acquired by the government.
predicates.adjacent_comparable_land_received_higher: Adjacent land in the same acquisition area with similar characteristics received higher compensation.
predicates.no_material_difference_in_land_features: The opposing party did not show a material difference in situation, topography or layout between the acquired land and the adjacent land.

issues.definition: When an owner appeals acquired-land compensation, comparable adjacent land received a higher award, and no material difference in land features is shown, compensation should match that for the comparable adjacent land.
